question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
answer:
No. When a creature phases back in (phases in), it does not trigger "enters the battlefield" abilities. Phasing is a static ability (rule 702.26a) under which, per rule 702.26d, "the phasing event doesn't actually cause a permanent to change zones or control... Zone-change triggers don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out." Since enters-the-battlefield abilities are a type of zone-change trigger (rule 603.6a), and phasing in is explicitly excluded from causing zone-change triggers, a creature's own "When this creature enters..." ability, and any other permanent's "Whenever a creature enters..." ability, will not fire when that creature phases back in.

This is because phasing doesn't actually move the permanent to a different zone at all - while phased out, the game treats the permanent as though it isn't on the battlefield, but it never actually leaves the battlefield zone (rule 702.26d). When it phases in, its status simply changes to "phased in" and the game once again treats it as existing (rule 702.26c), but no zone change ever occurred, so there's nothing for a zone-change trigger to key off of.

As a related point, if the permanent is an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification that phases back in while attached to something, that attachment doesn't count as it becoming newly attached either - rule 702.26j specifically states that abilities which trigger on a permanent becoming attached or unattached don't trigger when that permanent phases in or out.

Zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out. Tokens continue to exist on the battlefield while phased out. Counters and stickers remain on a permanent while it’s phased out. Effects that check a phased-in permanent’s history won’t treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to leave or enter the battlefield or its controller’s control.

question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
answer:
When a creature has both trample and deathtouch, the deathtouch ability changes what counts as "lethal damage" for trample's damage-assignment rules, letting the attacker send only 1 damage to each blocking creature and dump the rest onto the defending player, planeswalker, or battle.

Here's how the two abilities interact:

- Trample (702.19a, 702.19b) requires the controller of an attacking trampling creature to first assign combat damage to the blocking creature(s) until each has been assigned "lethal damage," taking into account damage already marked and damage being assigned by other creatures in the same step. Only after that can excess damage be assigned to the player, planeswalker, or battle being attacked.
- Deathtouch (702.2c) states that "any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered to be lethal damage for the purposes of determining if excess damage is being dealt." This applies regardless of the blocking creature's actual toughness.

So if a creature has both trample and deathtouch, its controller only needs to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature to satisfy the "lethal damage" requirement under rule 702.19b, and every point of damage beyond that 1-per-blocker can be assigned to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle instead. This is a case of a combination of abilities changing the normal outcome, rather than either ability's rule text being overridden.

Once combat damage is actually dealt, the deathtouch rules (702.2b, 704.5h) separately cause any creature that was dealt any damage by a deathtouch source to be destroyed as a state-based action, as long as its toughness is greater than 0, regardless of how much damage it took or whether it would otherwise have survived.

Note: the trample assignment process itself (deciding how much damage to assign where) happens during the combat damage assignment turn-based action, described in rule 510.1, before damage is actually dealt; the deathtouch-destruction state-based action happens afterward, once damage has been marked. This answer assumes the normal case where the trampling/deathtouch creature is legally blocked by one or more creatures still in combat when damage is assigned; if a blocker is removed from combat first, rule 702.19d instead lets all the trampler's damage go through to the defending player/planeswalker as though blockers had been assigned lethal damage.

Once all those blocking creatures are assigned lethal damage, any excess damage is assigned as its controller chooses among those blocking creatures and the player, planeswalker, or battle the creature is attacking. When checking for assigned lethal damage, take into account damage already marked on the creature and damage from other creatures that’s being assigned during the same combat damage step, but not any abilities or effects that might change the amount of damage that’s actually dealt. The attacking creature’s controller need not assign lethal damage to all those blocking creatures but in that case can’t assign any damage to the player or planeswalker it’s attacking. A 2/2 creature that can block an additional creature blocks two attackers: a 1/1 with no abilities and a 3/3 with trample. The active player could assign 1 damage from the first attacker and 1 damage from the second to the blocking creature, and 2 damage to the defending player from the creature with trample. A 6/6 green creature with trample is blocked by a 2/2 creature with protection from green. The attacking creature’s controller must assign at least 2 damage to the blocker, even though that damage will be prevented by the blocker’s protection ability. The attacking creature’s controller can divide the rest of the damage as they choose between the blocking creature and the defending player.

question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
answer:
Yes—Storm is a triggered ability, and like any triggered ability on the stack it can be countered, but only by an effect that specifically says it counters abilities (or targets it with something like Ward). It cannot be countered by an effect that counters only spells.

Storm (as printed on cards with the keyword) reads: "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies" [Storm][702.40a]. This is explicitly a triggered ability that functions on the stack [702.40a]. Rule [113.9] states that activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells, so anything that only counters spells (e.g., a generic "counter target spell") can't touch a Storm trigger. However, [113.9] also says such abilities on the stack CAN be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. A permanent's Ward ability, for example, is itself a triggered ability that can counter spells or abilities targeting that permanent [Ward], so if a Storm trigger targeted a permanent with Ward, Ward could counter it (though note the copies made by Storm are separate objects and would each need to be dealt with).

Also worth noting: if a card has multiple instances of Storm, each one triggers and exists on the stack separately [702.40b], so each copy-trigger would need to be countered individually by an ability-countering effect if you wanted to stop all of them.

Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Static abilities don’t use the stack and thus can’t be countered at all.

question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
answer:
No. A card with a hybrid mana symbol like {R/G} counts as both of those colors for color-identity purposes, even though the mana cost can be paid with just one of those colors of mana. Rule [202.2d] states that an object with one or more hybrid mana symbols in its mana cost is all of the colors of those symbols. Since Commander deck construction uses color identity — defined in [903.4] and [903.4f] as the color(s) of any mana symbols in a card's mana cost or rules text — a card containing {R/G} has both red and green in its color identity, regardless of how it's actually paid for. Rule [107.4e] confirms a hybrid symbol such as {R/G} 'is all of its component colors.' So under the deck-construction rule [903.5c] (illustrated with Wort, the Raidmother), if your commander's color identity is only red (no green), a card with a {R/G} hybrid symbol cannot be included, because green isn't in the commander's color identity — even though you could always pay the card's cost using only red mana. The same logic applies to monocolored hybrid symbols like {2/R} (which is just red) versus symbols like {C/R} or two-color hybrids like {W/U} — you need every color that appears in any hybrid symbol on the card to be part of your commander's color identity, not just one option from each symbol.

This is a two-player-agnostic rule — it's a deck-building restriction that applies the same regardless of how many players are at the table, since it's about what colors a card contributes to color identity, not about turn order or targeting.

question: can I respond to the untap step?
answer:
No. You cannot respond to anything happening during the untap step because no player receives priority during that step, as stated in rule [502.4] and reinforced by [117.3a]: "No player receives priority during the untap step." Since priority is what lets a player cast spells, activate abilities, or take other actions ([117.1]), and nobody has priority, there is no window to respond to phasing, the day/night check, or the untapping of permanents.

The untap step's events are all turn-based actions that happen automatically without using the stack: first, phasing occurs ([502.1], [703.4a]); second, the day/night designation is checked if applicable ([502.2], [703.4b], [731.2]); and third, the active player untaps their permanents ([502.3], [703.4c]). None of these use the stack, so there is nothing to respond to even if you wanted to.

If something triggers during the untap step (for example, an ability that triggers on a permanent phasing in or out), that triggered ability does not go on the stack immediately. Instead, it is held until the next time a player would receive priority - normally the upkeep step - at which point it's put on the stack before the active player gets priority ([502.4], [503.1a]). Also note that no game events can occur between steps, phases, or turns ([500.12]), and a step with no priority (like the untap step) simply ends once all its specified actions are completed ([500.3]).

This holds true regardless of how many players are in the game, since none of these untap-step rules differentiate between two-player and multiplayer games - the active player is always the only one whose permanents phase and untap during their own untap step.

question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
answer: Yes. Attacking creatures remain attacking creatures throughout the end of combat step. Per the definition of Attacking Creature, a creature "remains an attacking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first," and this is echoed in rules 508.1k and 508.4/508.4d. The end of combat step is the fifth and final step of the combat phase (per the End of Combat Step entry), so being in that step does not by itself end the combat phase — the creatures are still attacking during it. It's only "as soon as the end of combat step ends" that rule 511.3 removes all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers from combat; at that point the combat phase itself is over and the postcombat main phase begins. So during the end of combat step, before it ends, attacking creatures are still considered attacking (and still removed-from-combat triggers like regeneration, leaving the battlefield, etc. per rule 506.4 would still apply the same way they would in any other combat step).

question: Do you cast lands?
answer: No. Lands are never cast as spells — they are "played," which is a special action, not the casting of a spell. Per rule [305.1], a player who has priority may play a land card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty; playing a land is a special action that doesn't use the stack (rule [116.2a]). Because it never goes on the stack, a land is never a spell, and this action can't be countered and players can't respond to it with instants or activated abilities ([305.1], [505.6b]). This applies even to lands that also have another card type, such as artifact lands: rule [305.9] and [300.2a] state that an object that's both a land and another card type can only be played as a land — it can't be cast as a spell (see also the [Artifact Land] entry). question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
answer:
Yes. The evoke ability creates a triggered ability that reads “When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it” [702.74a]. Like any triggered ability, it triggers as soon as the creature enters the battlefield and is placed on the stack, but it doesn't resolve immediately — players get a chance to act (cast spells, activate abilities, etc.) before it resolves. During that window, nothing stops you from sacrificing the same creature to pay for a different cost or ability (for example, an activated ability that costs "Sacrifice a creature," an Exploit ability, or any other sacrifice outlet).

If you do sacrifice the creature that way before its evoke trigger resolves, the evoke trigger still resolves afterward, but its instruction to sacrifice "it" can no longer be carried out because the creature is no longer on the battlefield — the intervening-if condition ("if its evoke cost was paid") is still checked and will be true, so the ability doesn't just fizzle outright, but the sacrifice instruction itself simply has no legal object left to sacrifice, so nothing further happens [608.2a]. Also note that the sacrifice you make to pay some other cost is a completely separate payment from the evoke trigger's sacrifice — one sacrifice can't be used to satisfy two different costs/effects at once, so you can't "double-dip" the same sacrifice for both purposes [118.10].

Assumption: this assumes the other sacrifice effect resolves (or its cost is paid) before the evoke trigger resolves. If instead the evoke trigger resolves first, the creature is already gone, and any later attempt to sacrifice it for another effect will simply fail to find a legal object to sacrifice.

question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
answer:
Yes. Keyword abilities are abilities (just written as keywords with reminder text), so an effect that causes a permanent to "lose all abilities" removes keyword abilities like flying, trample, deathtouch, banding, etc., along with any other granted or printed abilities.

Rule 702.1d confirms that a keyword like "flying" is shorthand for having "a flying ability" - it's an ability, not a separate kind of thing. Rule 113.10 (and 113.10b) states that effects which remove abilities "remove all instances of it," and a "loses all abilities" effect works the same way at a broader scale, stripping every ability the permanent has, keyworded or fully spelled-out.

A couple of nuances worth flagging: (1) Statements that merely describe a quality of an object (e.g., "this creature can't be blocked") or that set a characteristic (e.g., "this creature is red") are not abilities under rule 113.12, so a "loses all abilities" effect does not remove those - only true granted/printed abilities. (2) Characteristic-defining abilities (rule 604.3) are still abilities, so they too would be stripped by a "loses all abilities" effect; if that removes the thing defining a creature's power/toughness, the creature would fall back to its default (often 0/0, per how CDAs work), so "loses all abilities" can have knock-on effects on power/toughness in those specific cases. (3) If the permanent has banding, losing all abilities also removes any "bands with other" abilities (rule 702.22b), since those are dependent on banding.

All of this is timing-independent of when the abilities were gained - whether keyword abilities were printed on the card or granted later by another effect, a subsequent "loses all abilities" effect strips them the same way, per rule 113.10b's "removes all instances" language.

question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
answer:
Yes. There is no rule preventing you from drawing cards while your hand is already at (or above) your maximum hand size. The maximum hand size only becomes relevant during a player's cleanup step: as a turn-based action, immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to bring it down to that number [514.1] [703.4n] [402.2]. This discard doesn't use the stack, and it only checks hand size at that specific point in the turn — it has no effect on your ability to draw cards at any other time.

So you can freely draw cards during the turn even if you're already over your maximum; you'll simply have to discard down to your maximum (normally seven, or a different number if something like a vanguard card's hand modifier changes it, e.g. a -1 modifier makes the maximum six [902.5b] [313.6]) once your next cleanup step begins, if you're still over the limit at that time. Note that this cleanup-step discard is specifically for the active player's cleanup step, so it's your own hand size at the start of your own cleanup step that gets checked.

Separately, if your library is empty, drawing a card (or being required to draw) is its own issue: you don't lose immediately just for attempting to draw with an empty library, but if you're required to draw more cards than remain, you draw what's left and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority, as a state-based action [104.3c]. That's unrelated to maximum hand size, though — it's about library size, not hand size.

question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
answer:
If a planeswalker has 0 loyalty counters on it, it is put into its owner's graveyard. This happens automatically as a state-based action, meaning the game checks for it continuously and applies it as soon as it's true, without using the stack (it doesn't wait for a spell or ability to resolve, and no player needs to do anything to make it happen).

Specifically: a planeswalker's loyalty is defined by rule [306.5c] as equal to the number of loyalty counters on it. Rule [122.1e] and rule [306.9] both state that a planeswalker with 0 loyalty is put into its owner's graveyard, and rule [704.5i] lists this explicitly among the state-based actions: 'If a planeswalker has loyalty 0, it's put into its owner's graveyard.' Because this is a state-based action under rule [704.1], it happens automatically the next time state-based actions are checked (which is done repeatedly, any time a player would receive priority), not as a triggered or activated effect that goes on the stack.

Loyalty counters get removed from a planeswalker in a couple of common ways: damage dealt to a planeswalker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from it (rules [120.3c] and [306.8]), and a planeswalker's own activated abilities can require removing loyalty counters as part of their cost when the ability uses a minus loyalty symbol like [-N], meaning 'Remove N loyalty counters from this permanent' (rule [107.7]).

question: do non-creature artifacts die?
answer:
No. Noncreature artifacts do not "die" — the word "dies" is a specific game term that applies only to creatures and planeswalkers, meaning "is put into a graveyard from the battlefield" [700.4] (see also the glossary entry for Dies, which restates this). A noncreature artifact that goes to the graveyard is simply "put into the graveyard"; it is never described as having "died," because that term doesn't apply to it.

This matters for a few related reasons: a noncreature permanent has no power or toughness, even if a printed number is on it (e.g., a Vehicle), so it can never be dealt lethal damage under the state-based action for lethal damage, which only checks creatures with toughness greater than 0 [208.3][704.5g]. It can still be destroyed if a spell or ability specifically uses the word "destroy" on it [701.8b], or it can leave the battlefield for other reasons (sacrifice, bounce, an Equipment/Aura becoming illegally attached and being put into its owner's graveyard by a state-based action [704.5m], a token ceasing to exist [111.7], etc.), but none of those events count as "dying."

If the artifact in question is also a creature — an artifact creature combines the artifact and creature card types [300.2] — then it does "die" when it's put into a graveyard from the battlefield, exactly like any other creature, because it meets the creature-toughness/lethal-damage rules [704.5g] and the definition in [700.4].

question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
answer:
You lose the game. If you (or an effect) would draw a card while your library has zero cards in it, you don't get a card, but as a state-based action you lose the game the next time any player would receive priority.

More precisely: rule [104.3c] says that if a player is required to draw more cards than are left in their library, they draw as many as remain (zero, in this case) and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority. This is implemented as a state-based action per [704.5b]: 'If a player attempted to draw a card from a library with no cards in it since the last time state-based actions were checked, that player loses the game.' Rule [121.4] states the same thing directly for the empty-library case. State-based actions like this don't use the stack and are checked continuously [704.1], so the loss happens as soon as any player would next receive priority (for example, after the current spell or ability finishes resolving), not immediately at the instant of the failed draw.

This loss condition applies to you as an individual player regardless of whether you're in a two-player game or a multiplayer game — it's not dependent on turn order or on how many opponents you have. In a two-player game, your opponent simply wins once you lose. In a multiplayer game, you're eliminated from the game and it continues among the remaining players (the provided rules don't give multiplayer-specific wording for this particular state-based action, but nothing here suggests it behaves differently with more than two players — losing is still just about that individual player's empty-library draw attempt).

A couple of related nuances: if the card is moved to your hand by an effect that doesn't use the word 'draw' (e.g., a tutoring or search effect), that's not a 'draw' at all, so this loss condition doesn't apply [121.5]. Also, effects that replace a draw (replacement effects) still apply even if your library is empty, and are checked before rule 121.4/104.3c would come into play for that particular draw [121.6a], [614.11]. And if you're deciding when this loss actually gets applied, note that the timing assumption above is that no other rule delays the state-based action check; if some effect were somehow preventing state-based actions from being checked, the loss would be delayed until they are checked again — but no such effect is indicated in your question.

question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
answer:
Combat has five steps, in this order (rule 506.1): beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat. The declare‑blockers and combat‑damage steps are skipped if no creatures are attacking; if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike, there are two combat‑damage steps.

As the defending player, you get priority in each step only after that step's turn‑based actions (which don't use the stack) have been completed, and the rules given only spell this out explicitly for the end of combat step: rule 511.1 says the active player gets priority as soon as that step begins, after which priority would pass to other players in turn order (you, as the defending/nonactive player, would get your chance to act after the active player passes). The other steps work the same way in practice (turn-based action first, then priority), but the specific rule stating 'active player gets priority first, then it passes to others in turn order' for steps other than end of combat isn't among the rules provided here, so I can't cite that for beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, or combat damage specifically.

What the turn-based actions look like in each step, for reference:
- Beginning of combat step: in a two-player game you're automatically the defending player (rule 506.2a); in a multiplayer game, if opponents don't all automatically become defending players, the active player chooses one opponent as defending player as a turn-based action (rules 507.1, 703.4h). If the 'attack multiple players' option is used with all opponents as defenders, all opponents are simply defending players from the start of the combat phase (rule 802.2).
- Declare blockers step: you, the defending player, declare blockers as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack (rules 509.1, 703.4j).
- Combat damage step: the active player announces how attackers assign damage, then you (the defending player) announce how blockers assign damage — in multiplayer this happens in APNAP order (rules 510.1, 703.4k, 802.5). Damage is then dealt simultaneously with no chance for anyone to act between assignment and dealing (rule 510.2).

question: can i respond to a mana ability?
answer: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities never use the stack, so they resolve immediately when activated (for activated mana abilities) or immediately after the ability that triggered them (for triggered mana abilities), without ever giving any player a chance to respond, target, or counter them [605.3b] [605.4a] [405.6c]. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated.' Rule 605.4a says the same for triggered mana abilities, noting they resolve immediately after the mana ability that triggered them, without waiting for priority. Since 'responding' (rule 117.7) means casting a spell or activating an ability while something else is on the stack, and mana abilities never sit on the stack, there is no window to respond to one — it's already resolved by the time you could react. Note that rule 605.2 clarifies an ability remains a mana ability (and thus still can't be responded to) even if it doesn't actually produce mana in a given situation. This is a general rule, not something that varies between two-player and multiplayer games — it applies identically regardless of player count.

question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
answer:
No. Paying a cost is not an event that anyone can respond to. A cost is simply an action or payment carried out as part of casting a spell, activating an ability, or performing a turn-based action such as declaring attackers or declaring blockers, and that payment happens all at once as part of that larger action, without the game stopping to let other players act in between [118.1] [118.2] [602.1].

For example, when the active player declares attackers, any costs required are paid as one of the steps of that turn-based action, and 'this turn-based action doesn't use the stack' [508.1j]. The same is true for the defending player declaring blockers [509.1e] [509.1f]. Because these actions don't use the stack, there is no point at which another player gets priority to respond specifically to the cost payment itself. Once the whole turn-based action (or the casting of a spell/activation of an ability, which follows a similar all-at-once process) is complete, the game moves on — for a spell or ability, it then sits on the stack and players get priority to respond to the spell or ability as a whole, not to the cost that was paid to put it there.

If a player is unable to actually complete paying a required cost partway through, that's not something an opponent 'responds' to either — it simply makes the entire action illegal, and it gets reversed: the action is undone, payments already made are canceled, and if it was a spell, it returns to the zone it came from [733.1].

So in short: you can respond to the spell or ability that results from a cost being paid (once it's on the stack, or once the attack/block is fully declared), but you can't insert a response into the middle of someone paying a cost.

question: can you explain layers?
answer:
Yes. "Layers" is the system Magic uses to determine the order in which continuous effects are applied to an object when figuring out its current characteristics (power, toughness, color, types, text, abilities, etc.). Rather than applying effects in whatever order they were created, the game processes them layer by layer, in a fixed sequence, so the same situation always resolves the same way.

How it works: an object's characteristics start from its "actual" values — for a card, that's what's printed on it; for a token or copy, it's whatever the effect that created it defined [613.1]. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a specific order of layers [613.1]:
- Layer 1: Rules and effects that modify copiable values (e.g., copy effects, mutate merging) [613.1a], [707.1], [730.1]
- Layer 3: Text-changing effects [613.1c], [612.1]
- Layer 4: Type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype) [613.1d]
- Layer 5: Color-changing effects [613.1e]
- Layer 7: Power/toughness-changing effects, applied in its own set of sublayers [613.4]

(The rules provided don't include layer 2 (control-changing), layer 6 (ability-adding/removing), or the specifics of layer 7's sublayers 7a-7d, though the example in [613.5]/[613.6] references layers like 2, 6, 7b, and 7c in practice.)

Within most layers, if multiple effects apply, they're sorted by timestamp — the effect that started applying earlier is applied first [613.7]. Layer 1 and layer 7 each have their own internal sublayers, and within each sublayer effects are still ordered by timestamp [613.2], [613.2a], [613.4]. Sometimes, though, a dependency system overrides timestamp order within a layer or sublayer — this happens when the outcome of one effect depends on whether another effect has already been applied [613.8].

A single effect can span multiple layers. For example, "gets +1/+1 and becomes the color of your choice until end of turn" is split: the color change happens in layer 5, and the +1/+1 happens in layer 7c [613.6]. Once an effect starts applying to a set of objects, it keeps applying to that same set in each relevant layer even if the source of the effect later disappears [613.6].

All of this happens continuously and automatically — as soon as an object's characteristics change, results "instantaneous"ly cascade through the layers. The classic example: Honor of the Pure ("White creatures you control get +1/+1") plus a black 2/2 creature. If something turns that creature white (layer 5), it now qualifies for Honor of the Pure's bonus (layer 7c) and becomes 3/3. If its color is later changed to red, Honor of the Pure stops applying and it reverts to 2/2 [613.5].

question: how does the legend rule work?
answer:
The legend rule is a state-based action: if a player controls two or more legendary permanents that have the same name, that player must choose one of them to keep, and all the others are put into their owners' graveyards. This check happens automatically as a state-based action whenever the game checks state-based actions (it isn't a triggered or activated ability, and no one can respond to it before it happens).

Key points: (1) It only applies to permanents that share the exact same name and are controlled by the same player at the same time — if two different players each control a permanent with that name, the legend rule doesn't apply to either of them. (2) It applies to any permanent with the legendary supertype, which includes legendary creatures, planeswalkers, artifacts, lands, and enchantments, not just creatures — the legendary supertype is what makes a permanent subject to this rule. (3) A legendary token created by an effect that says 'create [name], a legendary...' is treated as a token with that name, so it can trigger the legend rule against another permanent with the same name. (4) A permanent's supertypes are independent of its other supertypes/types — for example, if something is legendary and also becomes a creature or loses creature status, it stays legendary and remains subject to the rule unless something removes the supertype itself.

So, concretely: if you control two permanents both named, say, 'Urza, Lord High Artificer,' the legend rule triggers as a state-based action, you choose one to keep, and the other goes to its owner's graveyard.

question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
answer:
Your creature doesn't die the instant the damage is marked. Damage dealt by a source without wither or infect is marked on the creature immediately when the damage is dealt (rules 120.6, 302.7), and if that marked damage is greater than or equal to the creature's toughness, the creature "has been dealt lethal damage." But the damage itself never destroys the creature — destruction happens only as a state-based action (rule 120.5). State-based actions are checked and performed automatically every time a player would receive priority, before that priority is actually given (rule 117.5), and this happens before any triggered abilities go on the stack. So in practice, the creature dies during the very next state-based-action check after the lethal damage is marked — which for combat damage is essentially immediately after damage is dealt simultaneously in the combat damage step (rule 703.4m), since the game checks state-based actions before letting anyone act (rule 704.1, 117.5).

Concretely: (1) the source deals damage, which gets marked on the creature (120.6, 302.7); (2) the total marked damage is compared to toughness — if it's greater than or equal, the creature has been dealt lethal damage (see the 'Lethal Damage' definition, and rule 704.5g); (3) the very next time state-based actions are checked (which happens automatically and doesn't wait for anyone to act, per 117.5 and 704.1), the creature is destroyed and moved to its owner's graveyard, unless something regenerates it. Neither the spell/ability nor the damage itself is what destroys the creature — the state-based action is (120.5).

A related wrinkle: even damage below lethal will destroy a creature with toughness greater than 0 if it was dealt by a source with deathtouch, again as a state-based action (rules 702.2b, 704.5h) — that's a separate check from the toughness-vs-marked-damage comparison.

This holds the same whether there are two players or more than two at the table; nothing about how or when state-based actions are checked changes with player count based on the rules given.

question: can I cast my commander from exile?
answer:
No — you cannot cast your commander card directly out of the exile zone under the normal Commander rules. Rule [903.8] only allows a player to cast a commander they own from the command zone (paying the mana cost plus the 'commander tax' of {2} for each previous time it was cast from the command zone that game). There is no rule granting a general right to cast a commander card from exile.

However, if your commander card is sitting in exile because it was put there since the last time state-based actions were checked, [903.9a] (and the corresponding [704.6d]) let you, as its owner, move it into the command zone as a state-based action instead of leaving it in exile. Once it's in the command zone, you can then cast it from there under [903.8], again paying any accumulated commander tax. Note [903.9a] only applies if the card was put into exile (or the graveyard) since the last state-based action check — so this is essentially automatic the moment it lands there, not something you can delay.

The only way to cast a card straight out of exile is if some other specific rule or effect grants that permission (for example, [601.3f] notes that certain effects let you cast face-down exiled cards, and [702.170d] lets a plotted card be cast from exile, and [715.3d] lets an Adventure spell be cast later from exile). None of those apply to a commander card sitting in exile just because it's your commander — the commander designation itself ([903.3d]) doesn't grant a casting permission from exile; it only tracks what counts as 'your commander' in whatever zone it's in. So the practical path is: let the state-based action move it to the command zone, then cast it from there.

question: what happens during the cleanup step?
answer: During the cleanup step (the second and final step of the ending phase), two turn-based actions happen, followed normally by no priority being given to any player. First, immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to reduce their hand size to that number [514.1][703.4n]. This discarding doesn't use the stack. Second, immediately after that discard (if it was necessary), all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end -- these two things happen simultaneously and also don't use the stack [514.2][703.4p]. Because of this, damage marked on a creature persists until this point; if a creature has lethal damage marked on it before cleanup, it remains destroyed by the state-based action that already checked for that, but the marked damage itself is wiped away here [120.6]. Normally no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated during it [514.3][514.3a]. This is one of the few steps that ends simply because all its specified actions are completed, rather than by players passing priority [500.3]. There is an exception, however: after the discard and the damage/effects removal, the game checks whether any state-based actions need to be performed or any triggered abilities (including ones that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step") are waiting to be put on the stack. If either is true, those state-based actions are performed, the triggered abilities are put on the stack, and the active player then gets priority so players can cast spells and activate abilities as normal. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, an entirely new cleanup step begins and the whole process repeats [514.3a][704.3].

question: when are state-based actions checked?
answer: State-based actions (game actions like a creature with 0 toughness dying, that happen automatically whenever certain listed conditions are met, without using the stack — see rule 704.1a) are checked continuously throughout the game, not on a fixed schedule and not controlled by any player [704.2]. Concretely, the check happens every time a player would get priority: before that player actually receives priority, the game performs all applicable state-based actions as a single simultaneous event, then checks again — repeating this until no more state-based actions are performed, at which point any waiting triggered abilities are put on the stack and the check repeats again; only once a check produces neither state-based actions nor waiting triggers does the appropriate player actually get priority [704.3][117.5]. This means the checks happen at the start of most steps and phases (after turn-based actions and before priority is handed to the active player) [117.3a], and also during the cleanup step, even though players normally don't get priority there: state-based actions are checked at that point, and if any occur (or a triggered ability is waiting), they're performed/put on the stack and the active player does get priority that cleanup step [514.3a]. There is also a special case for effects that end the combat phase (such as an effect that says 'end the combat phase'), where state-based actions are checked as part of that specific process without any player getting priority and without triggered abilities being put on the stack [724.2c]. Note that state-based actions ignore what's happening mid-resolution of a spell or ability — they only look at the game state that exists once no spell or ability is currently resolving and priority is about to be given, i.e., between resolutions [704.4].

question: when can I concede a game?
answer: You can concede at any time. Per rule 104.3a, a player may concede at any point in the game, and doing so causes that player to leave the game immediately and lose it. This applies even in unusual circumstances: rule 723.6 confirms that even if another player is controlling you (e.g., via a mind-control-type effect), that controller cannot force you to concede, but you yourself may still concede at any time. Conceding doesn't use the stack (rule 405.6g) — it takes effect immediately, not as a spell or ability that could be responded to. It's also the one thing that always works even if a card's text seems to contradict it: rule 101.1 explicitly carves out conceding as the sole exception to 'card text overrides the rules.' In a Two-Headed Giant game (two-player teams), if one player concedes, their entire team leaves the game and the team loses (rule 810.8b), whereas in a standard multiplayer or one-on-one game, only the conceding player themselves leaves and loses (rule 104.3a). If conceding causes all remaining players (or in team variants, all remaining teams) to lose at the same moment, the game is a draw instead of a loss for any one side (rules 104.4a, 104.4d).

question: how do I know who the active player is?
answer:
The active player is simply the player whose turn it currently is. Per rule [102.1], "The active player is the player whose turn it is. The other players are nonactive players." This is also confirmed in the glossary entry [Active Player], which states: "The player whose turn it is. See rule 102.1."

So at any point during a turn, you look at whose turn it is (i.e., who is progressing through the phases and steps of their own turn), and that person is the active player — everyone else at the table is a nonactive player for that turn.

A few nuances depending on the situation:
- If a player is being controlled by another player during their own turn (e.g., due to a mind-control effect), the controlled player is still considered the active player — only control of that player's actions changes, per rule [723.3].
- In games using the shared team turns option, it's not an individual active player but an active team — the team whose turn it is — with each other team being a nonactive team, per rule [805.4a].
- Some abilities refer to "the active player" as a concept the ability's controller gets to choose among multiple active players (this comes up in specific multiplayer variants); rule [805.9] covers that edge case, though it doesn't change the basic definition — it's about which active player an ability refers to when there could be more than one.

The active player matters practically because they get priority first in many phases and steps (e.g., untap step is skipped for priority purposes, but see [504.2], [507.2], [508.2], [509.2], [510.3], [505.6] for various steps where "the active player gets priority" first), and because APNAP order (rule [101.4] / [101.4e]) has the active player make choices before nonactive players when multiple players need to choose or act simultaneously.

This explanation holds for both two-player and multiplayer games: the basic definition of active player (whoever's turn it is) doesn't change with player count. What can change in multiplayer is things like who becomes the defending player during combat — rule [507.1] notes that in a multiplayer game where opponents don't all automatically become defending players, the active player must choose one opponent to be the defending player, which is different from two-player games where the single opponent automatically becomes the defending player per rule [506.2].

question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
answer:
The player who cast the spell gets priority first — not the active player. Rule [117.3c] states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward. So if a non-active player has priority (for example, after the active player passes priority) and casts a spell, that same non-active player receives priority again once the casting is complete, before anyone else gets a chance to act.

This matters because casting a spell doesn't automatically hand priority to the active player — priority instead returns to whoever just cast the spell, regardless of whether that player is active or not. Only after that spell resolves does priority pass to the active player by default: rule [117.3b] specifies that the active player receives priority after a spell or ability (other than a mana ability) resolves. This same 'active player gets priority after resolution' pattern shows up repeatedly for various steps and phases (e.g., [504.2], [507.2], [508.2], [509.2], [510.3], [505.6]), confirming that the active-player-gets-priority rule applies specifically to the point *after* something resolves, not to the moment right after something is cast.

So to be precise about the two readings of your question: right after the spell is cast (before it resolves), priority goes to the casting player again per [117.3c]. Right after that spell resolves, priority goes to the active player per [117.3b]. This holds in both two-player and multiplayer games — none of the cited rules distinguish based on player count for this particular priority sequencing.

question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
answer:
Yes. If you have priority when you cast a spell, you get priority right back afterward, so you can keep casting additional spells (or activating abilities) before anyone else acts — this is commonly called "holding priority."

Mechanically: casting a spell is a multi-step process (moving the card to the stack, determining and paying costs, etc.) under rule [601.2a] and [601.2f]. Once that process is complete, rule [117.3c] says that if you had priority when you cast the spell, you receive priority afterward. This is echoed in [601.2i], which states that a spell's controller who had priority before casting it gets priority back once the spell has been cast. Because you still have priority, nothing forces you to pass — you may immediately cast another spell (or activate an ability, or take a special action) targeting the same or a different object.

When you do this, rule [117.7] confirms that the new spell is cast "in response to" the earlier one and will resolve first, since spells and abilities resolve in a last-in-first-out order on the stack. You can keep stacking spells this way as many times as you like, as long as you're legally able to cast each one (you have the mana, timing restrictions are met, etc., per [601.3]). The phase or step won't end and nothing on the stack will resolve until the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, per [500.2] — so as long as you keep holding priority and adding to the stack, resolution is delayed.

This applies the same way whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game with more than two players — priority itself, and the ability to hold it, isn't affected by player count in a normal game. One caveat: in the Grand Melee multiplayer variant, which uses multiple stacks rather than one, rule [807.5b] requires you to specify which stack each new spell or ability goes on, and certain restrictions apply about which stack a triggered ability or targeted spell must join — but the underlying ability to hold priority and cast multiple spells before passing still works the same way, just distributed across the relevant stack(s).

question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
answer:
Lore counters get added to Sagas at two distinct times. First, when a Saga enters the battlefield, it gets its starting lore counter(s) via a replacement effect: a Saga without read ahead enters with one lore counter on it [714.3a], while a Saga with read ahead enters with a number of lore counters equal to a number its controller chooses between one and the Saga's final chapter number [714.3b, 702.155a, 702.155b]. These replacement effects apply as the permanent enters the battlefield, not afterward [614.1c].

Second, on every subsequent turn, as soon as the active player's precombat main phase begins, that player puts one additional lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities. This is a turn-based action — it happens automatically and doesn't use the stack [505.4, 703.4f, 714.3c]. Note that only the active player's own precombat main phase triggers this for their Sagas; a Saga sitting under a non-active player's control does not get a counter added on someone else's turn.

Each time one or more lore counters are added (whether from entering the battlefield or from this turn-based action), the game checks whether the new total crossed the threshold for a chapter symbol's Roman numeral; if so, that chapter's triggered ability triggers [107.15a, 714.2b]. If read ahead applies, chapter abilities can't trigger the turn the Saga entered unless the Saga has exactly the number of lore counters specified by that chapter symbol [702.155a].

Finally, as a state-based action, once a Saga's lore counters equal or exceed its final chapter number (and no chapter ability from it is still triggered-but-unresolved), its controller sacrifices it [704.5s, 714.4].

In an Archenemy game, the lore-counter turn-based action happens after the archenemy's scheme action [703.4f].

question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
answer:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect—typically when a spell or ability resolves, or when a replacement effect is applied—that doesn't do anything immediately, but instead sets up a condition to trigger and act at some later point in the game. Per the Glossary entry for [Delayed Triggered Ability] and [603.7], it "contains 'when,' 'whenever,' or 'at,' although that word won't usually begin the ability," and it's created during the resolution of a spell or ability, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or as a result of a static ability that allows a player to take an action ([603.7a]).

A classic example is text like "Exile this creature at the beginning of the next end step" — the exiling doesn't happen right away when the ability resolves; instead it creates a delayed triggered ability that waits for the stated later trigger event (the next end step) and then fires ([603.7c], [603.7a]).

Key rules about how delayed triggered abilities work:
- They won't trigger until they've actually been created, even if the trigger event already happened just before ([603.7a]). If the triggering event becomes impossible before the delayed ability is even created, it simply never triggers.
- Normally a delayed triggered ability only triggers once, the next time its trigger event occurs, unless it has a stated duration like "this turn" ([603.7b]).
- The source and controller of a delayed triggered ability depend on what created it: if a spell created it, the source is that spell and the controller is whoever controlled the spell as it resolved ([603.7d]); if another activated or triggered ability created it, the source and controller match that ability ([603.7e]); if a static ability generating a replacement effect created it, the source is the object with that static ability and the controller is whoever controlled that object when the replacement effect was applied ([603.7f]); if a static ability that lets a player take an action created it, the source is the object with that static ability and the controller is whoever controlled it when the action was taken ([603.7g]).
- A delayed triggered ability that refers to a specific object keeps affecting that object even if its characteristics change, but if the object has left the zone it's expected to be in by the time the ability would resolve, the ability does nothing — a returned object is a new object per [400.7] and won't count ([603.7c]).
- One-shot effects commonly create delayed triggered abilities to do something later rather than immediately as the effect resolves ([610.2]).

A related but distinct concept is the "reflexive triggered ability" ([603.12]), which also follows the delayed-trigger rules but is checked immediately after being created, based on whether its trigger event already happened during the resolution of the ability that created it (e.g., "When you do," as on Heart-Piercer Manticore).

An example from the provided card data: Earthbend N creates the land-animating effect, and "when that land dies or is put into exile, return it to the battlefield tapped under your control" is a delayed triggered ability created as part of resolving the earthbend effect ([701.66a], [701.66b]).

question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
answer:
Yes. Non-permanent spells (instants and sorceries) can have abilities, but most of the text on them is a special kind called a "spell ability": per [113.3a], any text on an instant or sorcery spell is a spell ability unless it's an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that fits the criteria in rule [113.6]. A spell ability is simply the set of instructions the spell's controller follows while that instant or sorcery is resolving (see the [Spell Ability] entry, restating [113.3a]).

So an instant or sorcery's rules text is almost always instructions for its resolution, not a persistent ability. However, [113.6] explicitly allows exceptions: normally 'abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack,' but some instants/sorceries can have activated, triggered, or static abilities that function in other zones (for example, abilities usable from the graveyard or hand, like flashback- or cycling-type effects) - these are the 'exceptions' rule [113.6] refers to.

When an instant or sorcery does have such an ability functioning off the stack, the general rules for that ability type still apply: activated and triggered abilities on the stack are objects in their own right and aren't spells, so they can't be countered by effects that counter only spells, though they can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities; static abilities never use the stack and can't be countered at all ([113.9]).
